notes: \cpara{Sums up the three posts before it, one per clause, through its links.}
\cpara{States the thesis as a warning: caring only about controversial science leaves ``a head stuffed full of garbage.''}
\cpara{Argues that the news covers only the frontier of science, where the evidence is thinnest.}

\cfact{Offered with ``often'' and no source. Later evidence fits it. Dumas-Mallet and colleagues (2017) traced 156 biomedical association studies that newspapers had reported: ``Only 48.7\% of the 156 studies reported by newspapers were confirmed by the corresponding meta-analyses.''}
\cpara{Describes controversies as problems hard enough that experts can still fool themselves, which is why they draw heated argument and attention.}
\cpara{Adds that, for outsiders, controversies are not even fun.}
\cpara{Compares taking sides in a scientific controversy to supporting a team; the link goes to ``The Two-Party Swindle.''}
\cpara{Lists what a good textbook gives, ending, with a hedge, in ``a reasonably good guarantee'' that what one learns is true.}
\cpara{Sets press releases against textbooks: fake explanations of results the writer did not understand and that ``probably'' will not replicate.}

\cfact{Part of this has later support. In 462 press releases from British universities, Sumner and colleagues (2014) found exaggerated advice in 40\%, exaggerated causal claims in 33\%, and exaggerated inference from animals to humans in 36\%. Whether the writers understood the results was not measured.}

\cpara{Describes science as discoveries built on discoveries, back to Archimedes, whose account of floating needs no later knowledge, and advises starting at the beginning. Archimedes' \textsc{On Floating Bodies} contains the first known statement of what is now called Archimedes' principle.}
\cpara{Urges reading elementary textbooks for fun, since ``simplicity is at the core of scientific beauty.''}
\cpara{Begins a comparison for starting at the frontier.}
\cpara{Completes it: starting at the frontier is like trying to jump over the lower half of Everest.}
\cpara{Grants, with a hypothetical about oncologists, that some controversies are important to know about.}
\cpara{Restates the thesis: science need not be controversial to be interesting.}
\cpara{Adds that science need not be recent either, and ends with a joke about a diet of science news.}
